segments.title: Mitsumasa Yonai’s quiet memorial
segments.body: The burial place and nearby statue are both quiet and understated, an arrangement presented as fitting for Yonai’s character. The statue sits in another temple and is somewhat hidden, reinforcing the absence of grand public spectacle. The Japanese tourist board and government are said to describe Yonai as the leader who saved Japan from total destruction, which makes the secluded setting especially striking. Yonai is portrayed as someone who solved problems quietly, often behind closed doors, while stepping forward when necessary. The burial place and statue are read as physical expressions of that reserved public style.

evidence.note: Clarke describes Yonai's burial place, statue, and preference for quiet problem-solving over public spectacle.

segments.summary: A walk from Mitsumasa Yonai’s burial place to his secluded statue connects their understated setting with his reserved public style.

segments.title: Yonai’s place in modern Japan’s story
segments.body: Long study can make historical figures feel almost like members of a historian’s family, and the visit is partly a search for reassurance that Yonai is remembered as he might have wished. The quiet memorial setting meets that expectation, and viewers travelling in Japan are encouraged to visit it. Yonai is described as an important figure whose name has been comparatively forgotten. In this interpretation, he helped create modern Japan and saved the country after the Second World War by influencing how the Allies treated it.

evidence.note: Clarke reflects on historical attachment, recommends visiting Yonai, and states his assessment of Yonai's postwar importance.

segments.summary: The closing reflection presents Yonai as an overlooked figure who influenced the Allied treatment of Japan after the Second World War.
